passage: When the bullock cart stopped at the gate, five-year-old Rukmini ran out barefoot, then remembered and stood still. She pressed her palms together and said, 'Vanakkam!' very loudly. Sangeeta Mami, climbing down with a bag of bananas, laughed and put a hand on her head. 'Nallaa iru, kanna.' Then came an old man Rukmini had never seen, his wife, and two cousins. Vanakkam, vanakkam, vanakkam. Each one patted her or smiled. By evening Rukmini sat squeezed between them on the verandah mat, eating murukku, as if she had known them forever.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta Mami bring?
qa.a: A bag of bananas.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel sitting between the guests on the verandah by evening?
qa.a: She felt comfortable and welcomed, as if she had known the new faces forever.

qa.q: What could the family do to help Rukmini keep enjoying guests?
qa.a: Praise her greetings warmly and keep them light and playful, so welcoming visitors stays a happy exchange rather than a test.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Mami feel when Rukmini greets her with folded hands at the gate?
qa.a: Sangeeta Mami probably feels welcomed and fond, which is why she laughs and blesses her.

grounding: Shows a young child greeting guests with folded hands, receiving pats and blessings, and coming to feel part of a larger welcoming circle.

passage: On Eid morning in their Toronto apartment, the door kept opening. Nour, five, stood beside Jiddo Siddiq in her new yellow dress and did what he had shown her: right hand on her heart, a small nod, 'As-salamu alaykum.' The first uncle bent down, said, 'Wa alaykum as-salam, ya Nour,' and pressed a coin into her palm. An old lady from the mosque cupped her face and murmured a blessing. By noon Nour was greeting people before they had even taken off their shoes, and Jiddo winked at her across the room.

qa.q: Who had shown Nour how to greet the guests?
qa.a: Jiddo Siddiq.

qa.q: What does Nour greeting people before they took off their shoes suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels confident and happy, enjoying being welcomed by so many people.

qa.q: What did Jiddo Siddiq do that helped Nour?
qa.a: He showed her a simple greeting, stood beside her and cheered her on with a wink, so she felt safe to join in.

qa.q: How might the old lady from the mosque feel when little Nour greets her?
qa.a: She probably feels warm and pleased at being greeted respectfully by a small child, which is why she cups Nour's face and blesses her.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who learns a simple respectful greeting for guests, receives pats and blessings in return, and feels welcomed by a wider circle.

passage:
It was Grandparents' Day at Little Steps school, and Madhuri ma'am had placed Devika at the door. "Fold your hands and say namaste to everyone who comes in."

Devika did it thirty times. Namaste, namaste. Most grandparents smiled. One old man in a white kurta put his hand on her head and said, "Khush raho, beti." A grandmother gave her a marigold from her plate.

By the end, Devika wasn't reciting anymore. She was running to the door.

qa.q: What did the grandmother give Devika?
qa.a: A grandmother gave her a marigold from her plate.

qa.q: What does Devika running to the door suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: Devika has become happy and eager, feeling welcomed by all these grandparents rather than just reciting.

qa.q: How could Madhuri ma'am build on this?
qa.a: Let Devika greet visitors again at other events, and chat with her about who blessed her, so the warmth grows with the habit.

qa.q: What might the old man in the white kurta feel when Devika greets him?
qa.a: He likely feels pleased and welcomed, and his blessing shows he enjoys the little greeter.

grounding: Shows a young child greeting guests with folded hands, receiving blessings, and coming to feel welcomed by a wider circle.

passage:
Tuesday: When guests came to see the new baby, Deepika, five, hid behind the curtain. Mummy had to pull her out to say hello.

Thursday: Mummy and Deepika practised with her dolls. "Namaste, Doll Aunty!" "Jeeti raho, Deepika!"

Next Sunday: Parveen Aunty from downstairs rang the bell. Deepika opened the door and folded her hands. "Namaste, Parveen Aunty!" Aunty patted her head and put a toffee in her palm. Then she touched her own forehead. "Adaab, beta." Deepika copied it, and they both laughed.

qa.q: What did Parveen Aunty put in Deepika's palm?
qa.a: Aunty put a toffee in her palm.

qa.q: How had Deepika changed by Sunday, and what feeling does it show?
qa.a: She went from hiding behind the curtain to greeting Aunty at the door, showing she now felt confident and welcome.

qa.q: What helped Deepika most?
qa.a: Practising at home with the dolls made the form easy, so with a real guest she could enjoy the pat and toffee instead of hiding.

qa.q: How might Parveen Aunty feel when Deepika greets her at the door?
qa.a: Parveen Aunty seems pleased and warm, enough to share her own adaab and laugh together.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to greet guests with folded hands and feeling welcomed by the pat and blessing in return.

passage:
The rain came down so hard that the Diwali guests arrived at the flat dripping and grumbling. The lift was broken, and they had climbed four floors.

Madhuri, six, stood by the door with her brother Raghav, holding a towel. As each guest came in, she folded her hands. "Namaste! Happy Diwali!"

Nanaji's friend, soaked and puffing, stopped scowling. He bent, touched her head, and said, "Bless you, little lamp." An aunty dried her hair and pinched Madhuri's cheek.

By the ninth guest, Madhuri was bouncing on her toes.

qa.q: How many floors did the guests climb?
qa.a: They had climbed four floors.

qa.q: Why was Madhuri bouncing on her toes by the ninth guest?
qa.a: Madhuri felt happy and excited, because each namaste brought smiles, pats and blessings from the bigger circle.

qa.q: How could the family build on Madhuri's welcome?
qa.a: Let her keep greeting at the door on festive days and thank her afterwards, so she sees how much her welcome helped.

qa.q: What might the rain-soaked guests feel when Madhuri greets them?
qa.a: They feel softened and welcomed; the scowls and grumbling fade after her namaste.

grounding: Shows a young child greeting guests with folded hands on a rainy festival night and feeling welcomed through their blessings.

passage: The doorbell rang in the Chennai flat. "Francis, guests!" called Amma. Francis, five, ran to the door and pressed his palms together, the way Amma had shown him. "Vanakkam, Uma aunty!" Uma aunty bent down and patted his cheek. "Such a good boy. God bless you." Francis turned pink. He brought her a glass of water, walking very slowly so it wouldn't spill. Later, when more guests came, he stood at the door waiting, palms ready.

qa.q: What did Francis bring Uma aunty?
qa.a: A glass of water.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when Uma aunty blessed him?
qa.a: He felt shy and pleased, turning pink.

qa.q: What does Amma's teaching do well?
qa.a: It gives Francis a simple greeting that brings him warmth from guests, so he wants to welcome more people.

qa.q: How might Uma aunty feel being greeted at the door by Francis?
qa.a: She probably feels welcomed and charmed by the little boy's greeting.

grounding: It illustrates a child greeting guests with folded hands and receiving blessings, growing a feeling of being welcomed into a bigger circle.
